lead: A phasor is a fixed complex number obtained by freezing a rotating arrow at t = 0; the rotating arrow is only the picture used to derive it. It stands for a sine wave of fixed frequency. Its length is the peak or RMS value; its angle is the phase. Phasor notation turns the addition of sine waves into the addition of complex numbers. This is used in AC circuit analysis, power systems and signal processing. In India, the same idea describes the phase difference between voltage and current in a household fan or a factory motor. The frequency stays the same, so the angle carries the timing information.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for peak and RMS values, and basic complex numbers (a+jb, r∠θ).

sections.h3: From a rotating arrow to a phasor

blocks.where: V<sub>m</sub> is peak voltage in V; ω is angular frequency in rad/s; t is time in s; θ is the phase angle in degrees or radians.

blocks.text: At t = 0 the sine has the value V<sub>m</sub> sin θ. Draw an arrow of length V<sub>m</sub> at angle θ, rotate it anticlockwise at ω, and take its vertical projection. The projection is the sine wave. Freeze the rotation and keep only the arrow: that arrow is the phasor V = V<sub>m</sub>∠θ. A full cycle is 360° or 2π rad. Phase difference is φ = θ<sub>1</sub> − θ<sub>2</sub>. If φ > 0, v<sub>1</sub> leads v<sub>2</sub> by φ; if φ < 0, v<sub>1</sub> lags v<sub>2</sub> by |φ|. Lead means the wave reaches the same point earlier in time. Example: sin(ωt + 90°) leads sin(ωt) by 90°.

sections.h3: Three ways to write a phasor

blocks.text: Use the complex plane. The horizontal axis is real; the vertical axis is imaginary. The letter j means √(−1), so j² = −1. A phasor has three forms. Polar: r∠θ, where r is magnitude and θ is angle. Rectangular: a + jb, where a is the real part and b is the imaginary part. Exponential: r e<sup>jθ</sup> (equivalently r(cos θ + j sin θ)). Convert polar to rectangular with a = r cos θ and b = r sin θ. Convert rectangular to polar with r = √(a² + b²) and θ = tan<sup>−1</sup>(b/a), choosing the quadrant from the signs of a and b. Example: 10∠30° gives a = 10 cos 30° = 8.66 and b = 10 sin 30° = 5.00, so 8.66 + j5.00. The angle can be in degrees or radians, but keep one unit throughout a calculation.
This chapter uses peak phasors: length is V<sub>m</sub>. An RMS phasor has length V<sub>rms</sub> and the same angle; never mix the two in one sum.

items: Write each wave as a phasor with the same magnitude convention.
Convert each phasor to rectangular form.
Add the real parts and add the imaginary parts.
Convert the sum back to polar form.
Write the time-domain sine with the sum magnitude and angle.

blocks.text: Subtraction uses the same steps with a minus sign. The figure shows the flow. Phasors add like vectors: 10∠30° plus 20∠−45° is not 30∠−15°. The correct rectangular sum is 22.80 − j9.14, which is 24.56∠−21.8°. Only same-frequency waves can be added this way; different frequencies need separate phasors. Some syllabi call this symbolic representation. For a series circuit, the same phasor diagram shows voltage and current with a phase difference; circuit impedance is covered in Chapter 2.4.

figure.caption: The flow turns two sine waves into peak phasors, adds their rectangular parts, and returns a sine wave. Notice that the correct sum angle is −21.8°, not the difference of the input angles.

spec.title: Phasors add like vectors
spec.aria: Flow from two sine waves to peak phasors, rectangular addition, a sum phasor and back to a time expression.

examples.question: Two voltages are v₁(t) = 10 sin(ωt + 30°) V and v₂(t) = 20 sin(ωt − 45°) V. Find v₁ + v₂ using peak phasors.
steps: Both waves have the same ω, so they can be added as phasors. The peak-phasor convention is used, so the lengths are 10 V and 20 V.
Angle = tan⁻¹(−9.14 / 22.80) = −21.8°. The real part is positive and the imaginary part is negative, so the angle is in the fourth quadrant.
examples.check:
import math
v1m=10
th1=math.radians(30)
v2m=20
th2=math.radians(-45)
x1=v1m*math.cos(th1)
y1=v1m*math.sin(th1)
x2=v2m*math.cos(th2)
y2=v2m*math.sin(th2)
xs=x1+x2
ys=y1+y2
mag=math.hypot(xs,ys)
ang=math.degrees(math.atan2(ys,xs))
print(round(xs,2))
print(round(ys,2))
print(round(mag,2))
print(round(ang,1))

traps: Never add peak values directly when phases differ; 10 V + 20 V is not the peak of the sum.
Keep peak and RMS phasors separate; if a sum is a peak phasor, convert to RMS only at the end with V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/√2.
Use degrees for both the given angle and the inverse tangent, or radians for both; do not mix 30° with π/6 in one sum.
Check the quadrant of tan<sup>−1</sup>(b/a); a negative real part needs +180°, so atan2 is safer.
Different frequencies cannot share one phasor sum; treat them separately in time.

quiz.q: Define a phasor and state what its length and angle represent.
quiz.a: A phasor is a complex number representing a sine wave of fixed frequency. Its length is the peak or RMS magnitude; its angle is the phase.

quiz.q: Why can two sine waves of the same frequency be added phasor-wise, while different frequencies cannot?
quiz.a: Same frequency means the relative angle stays fixed, so complex addition gives the correct amplitude and phase. Different frequencies have a changing relative phase, so one phasor pair cannot represent the sum.

quiz.q: v₁ = 6 sin(ωt) V and v₂ = 8 sin(ωt + 90°) V. Find v₁ + v₂ as a peak phasor and as a time expression.
v = 10 sin(ωt + 30°) V and i = 5 sin(ωt − 20°) A. Which leads and by how much?
quiz.a: v leads i by 30° − (−20°) = 50°. A positive phase difference means v reaches a given point earlier.

quiz.q: A student writes 10∠30° + 20∠−45° = 30∠−15°. Identify the error and give the correct result.
quiz.a: The student added magnitudes and angles separately. Convert to rectangular: 8.66 + j5.00 and 14.14 − j14.14; sum = 22.80 − j9.14 = 24.56∠−21.8°.

beyond: Not for the exam. In power systems, phasor measurement units compare voltage and current phasors across the grid, timestamped by GPS; these are called synchrophasors. In signal processing, the same complex exponential r e<sup>jθ</sup> leads to the Fourier transform. In modern drives, controllers compute phasors to estimate motor flux and torque.
